Four Incident Circles

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: four equal circles all pass through one point, and four straight lines form a shape around them.
How to play: Drag any centre, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick Hint for the helper lines, tick Show names for labels, and press Reset to start over.
Look for the math

Drag a centre and all four circles change, yet the four corners where the straight tangent lines meet stay on one circle. Here is why the old page's droodle works, and where it needs a small caution.

Four centres on one circle

The red dot is the point all four circles pass through. When you drag one centre, the applet slides the other three along the rays from that dot so every centre is the same distance R from it. So the four centres are concyclic: they sit on a circle of radius R about the red dot. Each of the four coloured circles also has radius R, which is exactly why it goes through the red dot.

Why the blue lines are parallel to the chords

Take two neighbouring circles. A tangent that touches both on the outside is the same distance R from each centre, just as the chord joining those centres is. Two lines at the same distance from the same two points are parallel, so each side of the quadrilateral points the same way as the chord between its two centres. That is what makes the inner shape of centres and the outer shape of blue corners have equal angles.

The fourth corner joins the circle

The page says the four centres make a cyclic quadrilateral, so its opposite angles add to 180°. The blue corners have the same angles, so they lie on a circle too: the green circle in the picture is drawn through three of them, and the fourth falls on it. The logic test tries over four thousand arrangements and finds the fourth corner on that circle every time (worst radius error below 0.00001 of a board unit). One caution: after a big drag the labels B1 to B4 may no longer go around the circle in order, so an angle formed by those labels in name order need not be one of the quadrilateral's inside angles. The corners are still concyclic; read them around the circle to see the 180° sums. If two centres come within one unit the applet drops a tangent, and there is no quadrilateral to speak of.

What the checks found

The old applet's methods were transcribed a second time straight from its bytecode and compared with this page's geometry after 1,200 random four-drag sequences. Centres, tangents, corners and circle agreed. The same transcription confirmed the page's claim “This quadrilateral is always cyclic” for every non-degenerate configuration tested, as well as the parallel-side and angle identities behind the proof.

Try dragging one centre right next to another: watch the tangent between them vanish, then move it back and see the green circle return.
